settings.title: Fresh pasta every morning, sauces that take all day

settings.editor:
Giulia opened Osteria in 2009 with her grandmother’s recipes and four tables. The tables have multiplied; the recipes have not changed. Every plate starts at seven in the morning with flour, eggs and patience.

We buy from producers we know by name, change the menu with the seasons and cook in small batches — when it is gone, it is gone.

settings.title: Four tables and a grandmother’s recipes

settings.editor: Osteria began in 2009 as a tiny lunch room on Via dei Coronari. Fifteen years later it is still a family place, just with more chairs.

image.alt: Four tables and a grandmother’s recipes

settings.editor:
Giulia grew up in her grandmother’s kitchen in Frascati, rolling pasta before she could reach the counter. After ten years cooking in Bologna and Lyon she came home to Rome with a simple idea: cook the food she grew up with, properly, for her neighbours.

She still opens the kitchen every morning, and still makes the ragù herself on Sundays.

settings.title: “Good ingredients, time and no shortcuts. That is the whole recipe.”

settings.editor: The menu follows the market. Artichokes in spring, porcini in autumn, puntarelle in the cold months.
Pasta, bread, gelato and desserts are made in our kitchen every day by the same small team.
Most of our produce comes from farms within 80 km of Rome, and we know every grower by name.

posts.title: How we make fresh egg pasta every morning
posts.excerpt: One hundred grams of flour, one egg, and ten minutes of kneading. The method our kitchen has used since the day we opened.
posts.content:
Every morning at seven, before the first delivery arrives, two of us make the day’s pasta. It is the quietest hour in the kitchen and the most important one.

The ratio

One egg for every hundred grams of flour. We use a mix of soft “00” flour and a little semola for bite. On humid days the dough needs a spoon more flour; on dry days a splash of water.

  1. Make a well with the flour on a wooden board and crack the eggs into the middle.
  2. Beat the eggs with a fork, pulling in flour from the walls little by little.
  3. Knead for ten minutes, until the dough is smooth and springs back.
  4. Wrap it and let it rest for thirty minutes before rolling.

Don’t rush the resting. The dough is doing work while you are not.

Giulia Ferraro

Rolling and cutting

Roll it thin enough to see the grain of the board through it. For tagliatelle, flour the sheet, fold it loosely and cut ribbons about seven millimetres wide. Shake them out and cook within the hour.

posts.title: A short guide to Italian olive oil
posts.excerpt: Peppery or buttery, early harvest or late: what to look for on the label, and the three bottles we keep on every table.
posts.content:
Good olive oil is the cheapest way to make simple food taste wonderful. It is also one of the most confusing things to buy.

Read the harvest date

Olive oil is a fresh juice. Look for the harvest year on the label and use it within eighteen months. The best-before date alone tells you very little.

Taste, don’t guess

  • A peppery catch in the throat means healthy polyphenols, not a fault.
  • Bitterness balances rich dishes like bean soups and grilled meat.
  • Milder, buttery oils from Liguria suit fish and delicate salads.

On our tables you will find an oil from Sabina, twenty minutes north of Rome, a robust Tuscan one for soups and a gentle Ligurian oil for the branzino.

posts.title: Five natural wines from Lazio worth knowing
posts.excerpt: The region around Rome is finally getting the attention it deserves. Our sommelier picks five bottles from small growers.
posts.content:
For years, wine from Lazio meant cheap Frascati in carafes. A new generation of growers is changing that, farming organically and making wines with real character.

Our five

  1. A Cesanese del Piglio that drinks like a light Burgundy.
  2. A skin-contact Malvasia with notes of apricot and tea.
  3. A sparkling Bellone, refermented in the bottle.
  4. An old-vine Frascati Superiore that ages beautifully.
  5. A rosato from the hills of Cori, perfect with antipasti.

Ask us for a taste. A good wine list is a conversation, not a test.

All five are available by the bottle, and at least two are always open by the glass.

posts.title: Saturday morning at the Campo de’ Fiori market
posts.excerpt: Where our vegetables come from, the growers who keep the best for us, and why we change the menu when the artichokes arrive.
posts.content:
Rome’s oldest market is busy with tourists by ten. By then we are long gone. Our shopping starts at half past six, when the growers are still unloading.

Knowing the growers

Franco has sold us puntarelle and chicory for twelve winters. Anna’s tomatoes come from a field near Latina and taste like summer until October.

Buying this way means the menu has to follow what is good that week, not the other way round. It keeps the kitchen honest — and interesting.

posts.title: Our summer tomato salad, step by step
posts.excerpt: Three kinds of tomato, good salt, torn basil and olive oil. A recipe so simple that the only secret is patience.
posts.content:
In July and August this salad is on every table. It has five ingredients and takes ten minutes, most of it waiting.

What you need

  • A mix of ripe tomatoes: cuore di bue, datterini and green zebra
  • Flaky sea salt
  • A handful of basil leaves
  • Your best olive oil
  • A slice of day-old bread, if you like

The method

Cut the tomatoes into different shapes, salt them generously and leave them for fifteen minutes. The salt draws out the juice, which becomes the dressing. Tear in the basil, add oil and serve with bread to wipe the plate.

If the tomatoes are not good, make something else. No recipe can save them.

Giulia Ferraro
